absent: How async fault work is queued, executed and moved to the done list outside teardown
Locking and synchronization for the pending async queue and done insertion path
Allocator lifecycle and object layout for async work, routing entries, memslots and stat buffers
Full VM destruction ordering and callers of each destroy helper
IRQ routing construction, lookup and update concurrency
Dirty-ring and coalesced-MMIO setup, sizing and producer-consumer protocol
Bus creation, registration and dispatch behavior
Device creation and per-device destroy semantics
Power notifier registration and suspend or resume effects
Conditions selecting each alternate no-op or counting variant
Uevent delivery guarantees and userspace handling
Complete x86 decode and execute flow including opcode tables and permission checks
Detailed semantics of each operand kind and attribute flag beyond field placement

findings.text: Per-vCPU async page-fault teardown clears both the pending queue and the completed list and resets the queued count to zero.
Dirty-ring teardown releases the guest-frame tracking array and leaves the pointer null.
Coalesced MMIO teardown has two build variants: release the single-page ring when present, or do nothing.
IRQ routing teardown releases the whole routing table during VM destruction when no concurrent user remains.
Completion-queue reclamation always ensures the associated work item has finished before returning its cache object, except for wake-all markers that were never queued.
Routing-table release tolerates a null table and otherwise frees every per-bucket entry before freeing the table itself.
Memslot-set release only acts on the secondary index because the same slot objects are shared by both sets, avoiding dangling references on the second call.
VM debugfs teardown removes the hierarchy and frees per-statistic buffers sized by the sum of VM and vCPU header counts, skipping everything when the dentry signals an error.
Bus lookup for destruction is only valid once the VM reference count shows no active users.
Device teardown assumes exclusive ownership of the VM object and therefore takes no VM lock while destroying every listed device.
Power-notifier teardown either unregisters the VM notifier or does nothing, depending on build configuration.
Virtualization disable has a counting form that tears down syscore, CPU hotplug state and arch state only for the last user, and a no-op form in other builds.
VM create and destroy notifications maintain global created and active counters and emit a device change event carrying counts, event kind, creator identity and optional statistics path.
MMU rmap statistics file release drops the VM reference held for the open file, and the arch helper installs that file under the VM debugfs directory.
Emulator register cache writes back only registers marked dirty through the operation callback, and invalidation clears both dirty and valid tracking.
SALC emulation sets the destination byte from the current carry flag state.
Weak arch hooks for pre-destroy and virtualization disable default to no action and may be overridden by architecture code.
MMU rmap statistics are exposed as a debugfs file supporting open, sequential read, seek and release with module ownership.
Async-fault completion unlinking is protected by the per-vCPU async lock, which is released across the potentially blocking work flush and free and then reacquired.
Global VM counters are updated under a global mutex, virtualization use counting is guarded by a usage mutex, while device and routing teardown take no lock due to exclusive destruction context.
Instruction descriptor combines a 64-bit attribute word, an intercept identifier, padding, a union selecting execute handler or nested decode tables, and a permission callback.
Nested decode helpers cover ModRM-group duals, legacy prefix variants, coprocessor escapes with low and extended tables, ModRM-dependent instruction duals, and 32 versus 64 bit mode duals.
Host-assisted ALU helper family varies operand width and operand sourcing across one, two and three operand forms, with a fault-tolerant variant for one source form.
Async-fault work progresses from pending queue to completion list to flushed and freed, with a wake-all shortcut that completes without ever entering the pending queue.
Virtualization usage follows first-user setup and last-user teardown, with intermediate users only adjusting the count.

Work items removed from the completion path must still be flushed because VM termination can race normal handling, and modular builds must guarantee no module code runs after the final module release.
Destruction-time device unlinking deliberately avoids RCU list deletion so a stray reader would observe a poisoned pointer rather than a silent reuse of freed memory.
Operand kinds are small integers from none through accumulator halves with 31 defined values, packed into 5-bit fields for destination, source and second source at distinct shifts with a shared mask.

Instruction attributes are bit flags covering operand width, alignment, string and stack classes, group and escape decoding modes, vector extensions, address decoding, privilege and mode restrictions, branches, shadow-stack effects and writeback suppression.

Arithmetic flag mask covers overflow, sign, zero, auxiliary, parity and carry; transfer types enumerate none, call or jump, return and task switch; REX components have values one, two, four and eight.
Reserved-zero mask for emulated flags is a fixed 32-bit value stated in the fragment.
VM uevent payload uses fixed keys for created count, active count, event name, process identity and statistics path, with event values distinguishing creation from destruction.
64-bit-only helper text is either preserved or removed at compile time depending on build mode.
